document.title: The Intersection of AI & Legal Reasoning

posts.content:
“Show me your receipts.” That’s the rule for trust accounting. 

It’s also how bar associations make lawyer work defensible when someone challenges it, and it’s exactly the model Clio’s Senior Manager of Academic Partnerships, Kenton Brice, thinks should apply to AI in legal practice. 

He makes the case in a conversation with Joshua Lenon, our Lawyer in Residence, on the NYC Bar’s new AI policy paper: if bar associations required lawyers to keep records of AI use, including prompts, outputs, templates, and workflow, AI use becomes defensible under scrutiny.

For their full conversation on where the NYC Bar’s AI framework works, where it can go further, and what bar associations should do next, check out the links in our comments. Let us know your thoughts!

posts.content:
Nearly every conversation I had at ILTACON last week circled back to one question: how do we operationalize AI?

I spoke to many firms who have spent the last few years experimenting, running pilots, testing point solutions, and trying different models. A really positive outcome of these experiments is that individual lawyers have developed incredibly effective ways of working with AI. But today, firms are building strategies on a deeper level, with a goal to turn those pockets of success into a system.

At some point, dozens of AI point solutions floating around a law firm need a framework around how they’re used. The firm needs to know where AI fits into their workflows, what context it has access to, what it can do, and how that process gets repeated consistently across the organization. That’s the work of operationalization.

It’s also a big part of what we built Clio Operate to do: give firms a way to encode how work gets done, then bring AI directly into those processes with the context and governance to make it useful at scale. See what that looks like: https://lnkd.in/gJ446xwt

posts.content:
We kicked off #ILTACON this morning with an update on Clio’s latest innovations and where we’re headed next.

It was just a year ago that we signed the agreement to acquire vLex around a core thesis: the best context creates the most capable AI, and the more AI can do, the more important that context becomes.

For large legal organizations, that context is everything. It’s the law, the matter, and the institutional knowledge that shapes how the firm works.

Today, we showed how those pieces are coming together. Vincent is moving directly into Clio Operate, bringing AI into the matter with the context to take on increasingly complex and agentic work. Docket Insights adds live court activity to the authoritative legal knowledge Vincent can draw from, while Studio, Skills, and Memory give firms more ways to bring their own expertise and ways of working into AI.

That foundation is also expanding where Clio can go. I am so excited to announce our move into the judiciary, with Pablo Arredondo joining Clio to lead our work building for courts and judges.

A year ago, we had a thesis. Today, the pieces are coming together across legal knowledge, matters, workflows, and institutions. I’m incredibly excited about what we can build from here, and how much further we can push what’s possible for the industry.

Stop by our booth (#611) to say hi to the Clio team, and to demo what we're building.

posts.content:
This summer, The Innocence Center had some incredible help from our youngest team member yet: Ava Uglesic, our intern, and Noelle S. Uglesic, Head of Revenue Operations at Clio.

Our relationship with Clio goes back to 2015, when we first brought their software into our practice.  Over the past decade, that partnership has grown into so much more than a software subscription; it's meant consistent support as we've scaled, adapted, and figured out how to run a nonprofit law firm well.  This summer took that relationship a step further: instead of just software support, we got human support, with Ava and Noelle spending time alongside our team in the office and even in court.

Ava spent the last few weeks diving into the details of our work, helping us migrate documents into Clio and seeing firsthand how difficult it is to build a case when the facts, evidence, testimony, motions, and case law accumulated over decades are scattered across countless files. We explored how Clio Work could bring that information together, connect the dots, build timelines, identify patterns and inconsistencies, surface relevant authority, and help attorneys spend less time searching for information and more time building the strongest possible case.

She even attended a hearing in Los Angeles for the Jason Guzman case, getting a firsthand look at what this work really looks like and helping us think through how technology can further support our mission. Although the summer portion of the internship is coming to an end, we're excited to continue working together and exploring new ways technology can advance our mission.

Thank you to Ava and Noelle for lending your time and talent to TIC this summer, and to Clio for continuing to show up for us in every sense of the word. Grateful for partners who invest in our mission this deeply.

#TheInnocenceCenter #FreeJasonGuzman
